column2: What does a hypothesis test assess, and what can it not directly decide?
column3: It asks whether observed data are sufficiently incompatible with a specified statistical model to challenge it; it does not decide whether a theory is true, an effect is clinically important, or bias is absent.

column2: Why is a p value not the probability that the null hypothesis is true?
column3: It is calculated by assuming the null model and all test assumptions: it is the probability of a result at least as incompatible with that model as the one observed.

column2: Why is a nonsignificant result not automatically a type two error?
column3: Type one and type two error rates and power are properties of a procedure under assumptions over repeated use, not retrospective labels for one result.

column2: Why does post hoc power calculated from the observed effect add little?
column3: It merely restates the p value; once data exist, the estimated effect and its uncertainty are more informative.

column2: When is a one-sided test appropriate, and why is that condition rarely met?
column3: Only when effects in the opposite direction would be treated as equivalent to no effect for the decision; harm in the unexpected direction is rarely irrelevant.

column2: Why can an odds ratio mislead as a measure of relative risk when events are common?
column3: Odds ratios approximate risk ratios only when events are rare; when events are common they can look more extreme.

column3: An estimate can be statistically significant yet too small to matter, or nonsignificant while still compatible with important benefit and harm.

column2: What goes wrong when an independent-group test is applied to paired data, and a paired test to unrelated data?
column3: The independent test wastes information because it cannot remove stable between-unit variation; the paired test invents dependence that does not exist.

column2: Why do many tests at a five per cent threshold require multiplicity control, and what do family-wise and false-discovery methods limit?
column3: With many true nulls the chance of at least one false rejection rises; family-wise control limits the probability of any false rejection, false-discovery-rate methods the expected proportion among rejections.

column2: How can convincing p values arise without deliberate fabrication, and what distinguishes planned from exploratory work?
column3: Choosing outcomes, time points, exclusions, transformations or models after seeing results exploits researcher degrees of freedom; prespecification, registration, time-stamped protocols and code separate planned work.

column2: Why is a significant result in one subgroup and a nonsignificant result in another not evidence that the effect differs?
column3: Evidence that effects differ across patient characteristics requires a direct interaction test, not a comparison of separate significance labels.

column2: Why can bias toward similarity falsely support non-inferiority, and how is this usually checked?
column3: Non-inferiority only requires excluding an unacceptable loss, so poor adherence or outcome misclassification that blurs differences favours the claim; intention-to-treat and per-protocol views are often both examined.

column2: Why does pooling systematically biased studies in a meta-analysis not yield a trustworthy estimate, however precise?
column3: Meta-analysis is only as meaningful as the studies' estimands, bias and heterogeneity permit, so a precise pooled estimate from biased studies remains precisely wrong.

column2: Why does repeatedly checking accumulating data and stopping when significance appears distort the evidence?
column3: It inflates false-positive probability unless the design accounts for it, and stopping early for benefit when few events have accrued can exaggerate the effect estimate.
